https://www.dw.com/en/gaza-ngo-reports-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NWf3 With much of Gaza either severely damaged or behind Israel's 'Yellow Line,' more than 80% of residents are estimated to be living in makeshift displacement camps Image: Dawoud Abu Alkas/REUTERS Advertisement A new report on conditions in the Gaza Strip says that the roughly 1.8 million Palestinians in Gaza, or 86% of the population, living in displacement sites often face inhumane living conditions. The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) published its findings on Thursday, almost three years after the October 7 terror attacks against Israel that triggered the war in Gaza , and a year after the phased October 10 ceasefire plan that was supposed to usher in the war's end. "The October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza was supposed to end civilians' suffering. Nearly a year on, it exists largely in name only. Displacement in Gaza has not ended; it has changed shape," the report says. The findings are based on group discussions with 195 people living in internal displacement camps across five governorates in Gaza. What did the DRC say about the Yellow Line? Entitled "Confined by Design: The Human Cost of Protracted Displacement in Gaza," the report accuses Israel of "a policy of protracted displacement" since the ceasefire deal was reached . One means of ensuring this, the DRC says, is the so-called "Yellow Line," which demarcates the area of eastern Gaza near the border that is controlled by the Israeli military and is, according to the report, creeping toward the coast. "In addition to protracted displacement for hundreds of thousands of people, the defining feature of the so-called ceasefire is the Yellow Line which continues expanding westward and swallowing up more land, effectively squeezing families into 30% of Gaza's territory," said the NGO's country director for the occupied Palestinian territories , Alan Moseley. The 'Yellow Line' devides Gaza into two sections Image: Omar Ashtawy/APAimages/IMAGO Other groups, including the UN, have also reported the westward movement of the Yellow Line, as has the Israeli government , although some details differ. Last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put the share of Gaza's territory inside the Yellow Line at 60% rather than 70%, but he also said the plan was to expand the area. The DRC report also said aid organizations "describe being unable to operate within several kilometers of the line, either due to access constraints or security concerns." It said that this led to crucial aid and supplies failing to reach displacement camps nearer the boundary. What did the report say about living conditions in displacement camps? The DRC and the Agricultural Development Association (PARC) highlighted a series of major shortcomings in the often informal tent shelters and makeshift camps that have sprung up amid Gaza's rubble, where more than eight in 10 residents are believed to be living. These included but were not limited to: 80% of respondents reporting shortages of water both for washing and drinking Displaced households relying on outdoor cesspits Multiple families sharing single latrines, increasing the risk of gender-based violence and abuse Rat and rodent infestations exacerbated by the unsanitary conditions Food scarcity and lacking infrastructure for cooking, increasing risks of burns or injury preparing meals Rapid localized spread of illnesses and infections. For instance, more than 4,000 chickenpox cases were recorded in Khan Younis displacement camps in July alone Lacking and overburdened medical facilities with only half of hospitals and just over a third of primary healthcare centers still operational Lacking or non-existent formal education provision for young people, now lasting almost three years in some cases Reports of security concerns, particularly among men, because of the continued presence of artillery strikes, drones and stray gunfire Safety risks posed by unexploded and undiscovered ordnance, particularly when trying to clear rubble or return to areas where people originally lived The report warned of growing risks of domestic violence, citing both limited and shared facilities, and deteriorating mental health of adult males in the circumstances Image: Mohammad Kuhil/Danish Refugee Council The Danish Refugee Council also laid particular emphasis on lacking site management mechanisms at displacement camps. It said only 36% of sites currently had a designated site manager, typically a national NGO, coordinating services and managing conditions. Sites with such partners "have a structured community channel through which a gap, such as a collapsing cesspit, a missing water delivery, or an unsafe walkway, can be identified, escalated, and resolved," the report said. Israel has not yet commented on the newly released report. What actions did the DRC recommend? The DRC and PARC issued a number of appeals and recommendations, some to "all parties to the conflict," most to "the Government of Israel, as the occupying power of Gaza" and others to "the international community" and "donors and humanitarian actors." These included: Completely upholding pledges to cease hostilities Ending attacks against civilians, humanitarian workers and medical personnel Guaranteeing humanitarian access and medical evacuation pathways Supporting the establishment of a UN mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations. The groups called on Israel to "halt the further expansion of the Yellow Line" and to "disclose its current and future route transparently." They also urged Israel to cease the construction of permanent military infrastructure in the area and to provide "credible assurance that current troop positions are not intended to be permanent." They appealed for fewer restrictions on aid access, particularly so-called "dual-use" restrictions affecting medical supplies, water, sanitation and hygiene items, pest control, rubble removal and fuel. The report also warned that political and donor interest in the situation had declined markedly in the year since the ceasefire, even though conditions had not improved proportionately. https://www.dw.com/en/eu-summit-to-focus.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OGao Germany's Merz reiterated his call for a reduced EU budget on arrival in Brussels Image: Harry Nakos/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement European Union leaders are meeting in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China. The summit is sure to include some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients. On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion , with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend. Here are the main topics on the agenda: Chinese competition in focus The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year. The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China. The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Merz and Macron wrote a joint appeal for a tougher line on Chna in the run-up to the summit Image: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/picture alliance Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc. Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion. The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness. Divisive EU budget The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement. Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds. "We are in very, very difficult negotiations regarding the future finances of the European Union," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has been leading the appeals for a leaner budget, said on arrival in Brussels. "We must significantly reduce the common budget compared with the commission’s proposals. No member state of the European Union can afford this," said Merz. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also said the proposals currently on the table were "simply not acceptable." Talks could theoretically run late into the night Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Italy's Giorgia Meloni is among the most vocal defenders of maintaining the traditional funds like cohesion payments, she told parliament on Wednesday that she saw "no contradiction between old policies and new priorities." The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year. Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all. Ukraine support The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting. "All of us in Europe want this war to end," Zelenskyy wrote after arriving. "And for that to happen, strong signals are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine." He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians. Macron only has a few more EU summits ahead of him as term limit and presidential elections beckon in France Image: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions. Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader. https://www.economica.net/pretul-graului.text: Home - Companii - Prețul grâului de panificație a atins un maximum al acestui an Tona de grâu de panificație urcat pe navele din portul constanța ( preț FOB) a ajuns în săptămâna 26.10-1.11 la o medie de 246,1 euro, după patru săptămâni succesive de creștere, arată date ale Comisiei Europene analizate de Economica. A ajuns astfel la un nivel maxim din aprilie 2026 încoace, ultima luna din acest an pentru care există date. În perioada similară a anului trecut, prețul mediu era de 219,9 euro, cu 11,9% mai mic decât acum, iar la început de noiembrie 2024 tona de grâu românesc se vindea, în medie, cu 219,5 de euro tona. În Banat, prețul DEPSILO ( prețul mărfii deja stocate într-un siloz autorizat, încărcate în camionul sau vagonul cumpărătorului, dar fără transport inclus) era de 204 euro tona, prag depășit ușor luna trecută, în Muntenia s-a înregistrat un record din mai 2023 încoace, prețul ajungând la o medie de de 221,8 euro, iar în Oltenia costul mediu a ajuns la 200,1 euro, cu peste 12 dolari mai puțin decât săptămâna anterioară. Cerealele din Constanța sunt pe locul trei în topul celor mai scumpe din Uniunea Europeană, după cele vândute în Lisabona ( 270 de euro preț DEPPORT – prețul mărfii livrate și descărcate în silozul sau magazie din portul maritim/fluvial , înainte de încărcarea pe navă) și Bolognia, Italia ( 261 de euro preț DELFIRST -prețul mărfii livrate la prima destinație indicată de cumpărător), Dacă analizăm grâul furajer, și acesta a ajuns la un preț maxim în Banat, respectiv 175,4 euro tona, DEPSILO. Este cel mai mare preț din luna august încoace. Este însă al doilea cel mai mic preț din UE, după Bulgaria ( 173 de euro, preț DEPPROD în Stara Zagora). Producția de grîu a României este estimată la 12,2 milioane de tone de grâu moale, față de 11,6 milioane de tone cu un an în urmă, conform datelor INS (12,6 milioane de tone conform datelor provizorii).
